q: Electrical energy can be transformed into a wide variety of other useful forms of energy.
e: Electrical energy is highly versatile and can be converted into many other useful forms of energy.

q: The transformation of electrical energy into heat energy is very useful and important.
e: Many home appliances rely on the useful transformation of electrical energy into heat energy.

q: Electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as resistors and capacitors.
e: Electrical energy is provided by sources of electromotive force such as batteries and generators.

q: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady potential difference is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.
e: Batteries and generators maintain the steady potential difference required for a steady current.

q: Batteries and generators are called sources of electromotive force.
e: These devices provide the electromotive force needed to drive current through a circuit.

q: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from electrical form into other forms.
e: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into electrical form.

q: A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.
e: The chemical reactions inside a battery generate electrical energy for the circuit.

q: In an electric generator, heat energy is converted into electrical energy.
e: In an electric generator, mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy.

q: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.
e: These terminals define the polarity and direction of the potential difference provided by the source.

q: The positive charges are sent from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the positive terminal within the source.

q: The main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the negative terminal within the source.
e: This internal movement of negative charges maintains the potential difference across the terminals.

q: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the complete circuit.
e: This is the exact definition of electromotive force in a complete circuit.

q: Electromotive force is measured in unit of ampere ($A$).
e: Electromotive force is measured in unit of volt ($V$).

q: One volt is equivalent to joule per coulomb of electric charge ($J C^{-1}$).
e: This equivalence defines the volt in terms of energy and charge.

q: Despite its name, electromotive force is actually a physical force.
e: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a force; it is a potential energy per unit charge.

q: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an internal resistance.
e: Real-world sources like batteries inherently possess some internal resistance.

q: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and temperature.
e: These physical and chemical factors determine the magnitude of a battery's internal resistance.

q: A battery which has an internal resistance $r$ must be viewed as a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in parallel to the battery.
e: A battery which has an internal resistance $r$ must be viewed as a resistor of resistance $r$ connected in series to the battery.

q: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the external resistor is $V = IR$.
e: This is the standard application of Ohm's law to the external load resistor.

q: The work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance $r$ of the battery is $Ir$.
e: The voltage drop across the internal resistance is given by the product of current and internal resistance.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR - Ir$.
e: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR + Ir$.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is the emf $E$ of the battery.
e: The sum of the potential drops across the external and internal resistances equals the emf.

q: The circuit equation is $E = I(R - r)$.
e: The circuit equation is $E = I(R + r)$.

q: The potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by $V = E - Ir$.
e: The terminal voltage is the emf minus the voltage drop across the internal resistance.

q: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always greater than its emf.
e: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals is always less than its emf.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the terminal voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.
e: This is the voltage actually available to the external circuit.

q: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: Electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in an open circuit.

q: Terminal voltage is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a closed circuit.
e: Terminal voltage is measured when current is flowing through a closed circuit.

q: Thus, emf is a closed-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is an open-circuit voltage.
e: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a closed-circuit voltage.

q: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by electrical energy from some external source.
e: An external battery charger provides the electrical energy to reverse the chemical reactions.

q: In charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E - Ir$.
e: In charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E + Ir$.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when open circuit (not in use) is $V = E$.
e: With no current flowing, there is no internal voltage drop, so terminal voltage equals emf.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when charging is $V > E$.
e: During charging, the external source must overcome both the emf and the internal voltage drop.
